subtopic: INVESTIGATION BY BOARD OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
INVESTIGATION BY BOARD OF TRANSPORT COMMISSIONERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to advise the house that the government has asked the board of transport commissioners to make a thorough investigation of the railway-highway crossing problem in Canada. For some time the government has been giving consideration to this problem which, because of expanding motor vehicle traffic and improved highways, has become one of national concern in respect of the present need for protection, safety and convenience of the public.
The railway grade crossing fund was established in 1909 under the Railway Act for the purpose of aiding in the actual construction work for the protection, safety and convenience of the public with respect to certain railway-highway crossings. From 1909 to March 31, 1952, a total of $13,327,000 was expended by the government of Canada through this fund. The annual amounts paid into the fund have varied from $200,000 in 1909 to $1 million at the present time. The act of 1909 provided for a contribution from the grade crossing fund of an amount not exceeding 20 per cent of the cost, with a maximum of $5,000 for any one crossing. The act of course was amended from time to time, and in 1950 provision was made for a contribution not exceeding 40 per cent of the cost where the total cost does not exceed $150,000 for any one crossing, and where the cost exceeds $150,000 a contribution not in excess of 40 per cent with a ceiling of $150,000. The contributions of other parties, such as railways, municipalities, counties and provincial governments, vary with each project as determined by the board after hearing applications for contributions from the grade crossing fund to eliminate or protect railwayhighway crossings.
As I have just indicated, the Canadian government has made substantial contributions through the railway grade crossing fund towards the railway-highway level crossing problem. However, it may be that certain restrictions in the existing legislation, and the present basis of contributions by the railway companies, the provinces and the municipalities, tend to impede the improvement and elimination of many grade crossings. In the circumstances, therefore, the board of transport commissioners has been directed to undertake a thorough investigation into all phases of the railway-highway crossing problem. It is our earnest hope that

their investigation, which will cover all ten provinces, will result in the submission of recommendations, the implementation of which will serve to effect a material reduction in the number of fatal accidents. I now wish to table order in council No. 52 which was passed this day.

speechtext:
Under the Representation Act, 1952, the entire constituency of Maple Creek was incorporated with a portion of the constituency of Swift Current and named Swift Current. The object of this bill, Mr. Speaker, is to preserve the name of one of the first constituency units in Saskatchewan, and certainly the most historical, in the name of Maple Creek. Having the two names, Swift Current-Maple Creek, designating the largest settled and most important constituency in this country, will be a source of satisfaction and pride, not only to those living in that area but to all of the people in Canada and, incidentally, make the seat safe for democracy.

That, in the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial governments for the purpose of providing pensions, equal to old age pensions, for all those who are incapacitated and unable to earn their living, regardless of age.
He said: Mr. Speaker, before I deal with the resolution I would like to welcome back to the house the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin). We would like to tell him, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), that we think they have been doing a creditable job at the United Nations. We just hope they will be long spared.
Looking at the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare, he is more like what he was when he came into this house-he has reduced considerably. Whether or not it is from sweating up in the committee, if he keeps on he will have a splendid opportunity of trying out for our big event in the spring.
Is that the election?

This resolution will be supported by my hon. friend the member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott) who has another resolution on the order paper similar to this. This is not the first time that I have brought this matter up in the house, but I hope it will be the last time that it will be needed. I am not going to speak long because I want it to go to a vote so that the house will know, and the government will know, that the people from coast to coast are interested in this matter. It is the most important resolution that will be brought before this house this year, because of its extent and because of the outstanding need.
I have received a great many letters which I am not going to read, because hon. members know the need just as well as I do. I have received long articles and a great deal of information from the trades and labour council of Fort William, as well as from others. I congratulate the government of Ontario upon going along the line of social security which we on this side of the house are following. We commend them heartily for passing legislation granting pensions to those who are incapacitated. Not only that, but I know there are cases where the help has really come from the province of Ontario and therefore, from one province at least, we shall receive wholehearted support on this question.
I might divide these cases into three classes. The first class of those who are

incapacitated might be those who are not able to work and earn a livelihood like the ordinary individual, but who can get around by means of a wheelchair. The second class would be those who cannot get around in a wheelchair or by any other means but who, when placed at a desk or a table, can use their hands, their, speech or their head to earn something. They cannot earn a great deal because there is a limit to the amount of goods which they produce that friends and other individuals can purchase. The third class, Mr. Speaker, with which I am most concerned are those who can neither get around nor earn a dollar. To me those individuals need to be fed ~and clothed; they need to have medical attention and nurses. They are just like newborn babies, the most helpless things in the world. I say, therefore, that the government of Canada should certainly take care of these people. Hon. members can see that this is a very important resolution. I am going to try to cut down my speech so that we can get a vote.
You have all seen the wheelchair brigade. We would not like to be there, and because we are not there we should be willing to help them. These people are more needy than old age pensioners; they are more needy than many of the blind, and more in need of help than those who get relief through unemployment insurance. I have wholeheartedly supported all these things in the house, but I will not support any other social security measure until there is provision made for these people. I include health insurance in that, for which I worked so hard for two years on the committee. This measure is needed more than health insurance for Canada. Some people think that these are the forgotten people, but they are not. The Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) last year informed me that there was a committee of the Department of Labour, national health and national defence, who are working with representatives in the different provinces to find a way of taking care of these people as well as the incapacitated veterans.
I realize that if the measure is adopted it will mean more taxes. I expect even the members of the opposition, who think we are so highly taxed, to support this resolution because I believe they are human and they recognize the needs of these people. I would just interject here that Canadians pay lower taxes than the people of the United States, Great Britain, New Zealand or Australia. When I visit some of these people I realize that one cannot help them merely by giving them something of one's own. It is a job for the Dominion of Canada. I know
Pensions for Disabled Persons the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is in his seat today because he wants to support this motion. He wants to let us have the benefit of his judgment. He is going to show us his warmheartedness by not allowing this motion to be talked out.
I should like to speak for an hour, but my common sense and better judgment tell me that I should allow others to have their say. Thank you for your consideration.

This resolution we are discussing today, Mr. Speaker, has been before this house on many occasions. I remember speaking on the matter and supporting it on at least two or three occasions.
I assure the hon. member who introduced the resolution that I am not going to talk for any great length of time. I want to see the motion voted upon, and I want to hear the minister make a declaration on the matter.
The resolution, as introduced by the hon. member today, is extremely broad, but the intention of it is to provide people who are disabled and unable to earn their own living with a pension. The phrase used in the resolution is:
-who are incapacitated and unable to earn their living, regardless of age.
This phrase is open to some criticism, but I am going to regard the resolution as favouring the principle of providing pensions to people who are unable to earn their own livelihood or who cannot be rehabilitated. These people are classed as totally and permanently disabled. Under these conditions, I am going to favour the resolution, and I think that the introduction of legislation along these lines will be a real advance and extension of our social security. It would fill a very serious gap. Public assistance is given to these individuals, and I will cite some forms this assistance takes. It takes the form of pensions under existing legislation. First in this class, I would put the veterans *legislation. Secondly, I would place benefits under mothers' allowance; then workmen's compensation and care in institutions for those who are chronically ill; homes for the aged; and hospitals, especially those hospitals for incurables. Lastly, there is the matter of direct relief from municipalities.
It is unfortunate that in Canada there is a grave lack of institutions of this character, especially of institutions for those who are chronically ill or incapacitated or even those who are classed as incurables. Very often people who are in this class are unable to procure any type of accommodation. Any person who has had any experience in trying to place a person who is incapacitated or totally disabled in some form of institution will understand that there is great difficulty in obtaining accommodation.

Pensions for Disabled Persons There is grave difficulty in obtaining an institution which is qualified and which can provide that type of accommodation. I am constantly receiving letters with regard to the matter which has been raised by the hon. member today in his resolution; and I am sure that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) also receives such letters. These letters usually take the same form. They inquire about the possibility of a pension for some member of the family who is disabled. I receive letters from parents who unfortunately have an invalid in their family, where the parents are becoming old and are worried about what will happen to the invalid when they pass out of this world. One can understand anxiety of this type when the parents, owing to the age they have attained, look forward to the future and wonder what is going to become of a son or daughter who is disabled and unable to earn a living. I have had personal experience in trying to place some of these people and I assure the house that, while the number of these cases is not large, there is still that difficulty in obtaining accommodation.
This brings us back again to the question of either hospitals for those who are chronically ill or hospitals where completely disabled people may receive some measure of care. I am proud that my native province of Ontario was the first of the provinces in Canada to introduce legislation of the type suggested by the hon. member in his resolution; and although legislation of this type has been in force for only a short time in Ontario, the benefits are becoming apparent and have been received as a blessing by those who are entitled to them.
When a measure such as that suggested by the hon. member is introduced consideration must be given to persons who are a burden not only to themselves but to their families and often to the community. Without financial assistance these people face a serious problem, and the financial burden is probably greater than the husband, the wife, the parents or the relatives can bear, and perhaps the community cannot give adequate financial help. Legislation of the type proposed in the resolution would alleviate these conditions, and the disabled person would have a measure of independence and would be able to pay his own way.
There will, of course, be certain limits with regard to incapacity and inability to earn a living, and these limitations will have to be defined. The definition of words like "incapacity" and "disabled" will involve some measure of difficulty, but a clear definition can be found if we study what has happened in the United States. In 32 states legislation of this type has been passed; but in those 

states rehabilitative or restorative treatment has not always been considered as part of the program. We are aware that at present a rehabilitative program is receiving some study in this country and we can consider the resolution as affecting those who have never participated in the labour forces.
Let me give some of the definitions of some of the states with regard to disability and incapacity. I will take first the state of Illinois in which the following definition has been approved:
An individual has a permanent disability when he has a physical or mental impairment, (1) irreversible or (2) progressive and not amenable to treatment, or (3) requires treatment which is extremely hazardous or of questionable benefit. The disability is considered total when it constitutes a complete handicap in relation to useful occupations within the individual's competence.
Then as to the state of Utah, I quote from their definition of permanently and totally disabled:
That the individual has some physical or mental impairment, disease or loss that substantially precludes him from engaging in useful occupations within his competence, such as holding a job or homemaking.
These are definitions that we shall have to study when we prepare for this type of legislation. Let me read the definition given by the state of Wisconsin:
A totally and permanently disabled person is a person found by medical authority to be so totally and permanently disabled physically as to require constant and continuous care.
That sounds like a really good definition. The state of Michigan grants aid to disabled persons under the following definition:
A disabled person is one who has a physical or mental impairment which cannot be corrected within the foreseeable future and who by reason of such impairment is unable, without help of any person, to carry on the minimum of activity essential to daily living as determined by the state social welfare commission.
The state of Vermont defines a disabled person as follows:
Crippled persons have been legally defined as persons crippled by the loss of limbs which prevents them from performing the necessary work to earn their maintenance when such crippled condition is due to the impairment or loss of function of motor or muscular activity due to disease or injury affecting muscles, joints or nerves.
It will be noted that there is a wide variation in the definitions of what comprises a totally disabled and incapacitated person, as witness the different definitions in the 32 states in the United States where legislation of this type has been introduced. But in all of those states it will be noted that they have restrictive definitions and generally do not consider restorative or rehabilitative treatment as part of their program. It is extremely difficult to estimate the number requiring such assistance. The rates in Canada

for disability and invalidity could not be considered accurate when estimating the number of cases. One must take into account the number of cases receiving assistance under such conditions as workmen's compensation or veterans' allowances.
May I ask a question?
Yes.
Has the hon. member the Ontario definition?
The Ontario definition is "totally and permanently disabled."
But what is the explanation of "totally and permanently disabled"?

A person is totally and permanently disabled-I am not quoting now but this is my interpretation-if there is not hope of recovery or if the disability is such as to preclude them from ever engaging in any form of gainful employment. That would be my definition. I have not inquired into the two words that are used, but those two words come into the Ontario act, and that has been my interpretation.
I was saying that as to workmen's compensation and veterans' allowances the number of persons who are benefiting under such forms of care would also have to be considered. The government of Australia has an insurance plan for invalidity, and the incidence in that country is 9 per thousand of population. I have not the incidence in the province of Ontario, for which the minister might ask, but the incidence in Australia under present conditions is 9 per thousand population. That might be a higher rate than we have in Ontario because there may be some difference with regard to social security legislation already in existence in Ontario as compared with that in Australia. Also Australia may have a higher rate than the province of Ontario on account of the number of people who receive care in hospitals and institutions. But when this plan was first started in Australia-and I think that was in the year 1910-the eligibility requirements were extremely generous and the number of recipients was estimated at the beginning of the plan to be two or three persons per thousand population. The program at present is wide in its scope and they have also had the experience of having an act that has been in force since 1910. The act in Australia is much wider in the coverage of cases than is the plan in existence in Ontario at the present time. However, there is this difference to be noted, as I said before. There may be in existence certain types of
Pensions for Disabled Persons legislation of the nature that I have suggested, like workmen's compensation and mothers' allowances which exist in Ontario, but which do not exist in Australia.
It would be rather difficult at the present time to obtain statistics from Great Britain regarding the coverage of cases, because it might be bound up with the national health plan which does exist in England. The program of aid to the disabled came into existence in the United States in October, 1950. In that country the federal government and the states share the cost 50 per cent each.
We could also give consideration to meeting the needs of disabled persons who reside with their families or with their relatives, and for whom the relatives provide care and maintenance. In some of these cases there is no doubt that the family is financially able to maintain the disabled person, but there are other cases where it places a severe strain upon the family and upon the financial reserves of either the relatives or the family. In these cases, if a disabled allowance were granted it would assist the disabled person to pay his own way, and it would allow him to retain his independence. In most of the cases of disability under consideration these people require constant and continuous care. It is not necessary that these people be placed in hospitals, because the acute phase of the disease, or the accident which has caused the disability, is passed. The patient may be cared for in his own home, and thus save expense to the relatives who cannot meet the expense of maintaining a case in the hospital.
There is no doubt that many of these cases are still remaining in some of the hospitals because the relatives have not had the money to meet the expense of maintaining them in their home. I point out that the maintenance in a home of a person who is physically disabled creates a problem, owing to the lack of facilities for nursing care and of the expenses involved.
There are certain physical disabilities which are caused by, or included in, some of the following diseases or injuries. I suggest some of these cases to the house for the purpose of clarifying the situation and to point out the need of these cases for special care. Hon. members will recognize, from the list that I am going to give, the urgent necessity of dealing with some of these things. I place in the first class various forms of paralysis, probably acquired in childhood, such as poliomyelitis or infantile paralysis and spastic conditions. I place also in this list diseases like cancer, injuries to the spine, probably by accident and not covered by workmen's compensation or insurance, or they may have

Pensions for Disabled Persons been born with some of these disabilities. Arthritis is a crippling disease. At the present time I think of one case which I saw the other day, which would come into this class, and which I think a pension would benefit greatly. Then there are various forms of amputations. Some of these can be rehabilitated. Then there are severe types of heart disease. Oftentimes the patient has no money and is unable to care for himself. It is a chronic condition and a pension would help these people a great deal. There are certain classes of epileptics, although there are epileptics who are taking their place in industry with guarded machinery, and are really doing a good job. There are others who are unable to earn their livelihood. I list these disabilities and I give the house these examples. I again emphasize the fact that many of these disabilities require almost constant care. A pension would meet the needs of a person who is disabled and it would be a great help to the family or to other people who have had to assume the care of these disabled persons. Municipalities give direct relief, but even this form of care cannot be considered satisfactory.
In previous debates on this resolution, or a similar one, in this house I have never heard a dissenting voice. Physically and mentally handicapped patients should receive care. That has been recognized by the house in all previous debates. It will be an advance in the field of social security, and I think people generally will recognize it as a necessary act. I have always felt that people who are disabled, such as those we have been speaking about and who have not had the benefit of good health, who may be physically handicapped and unable to maintain themselves, should be placed in the welfare group. When the Old Age Security Act was passed we recognized the needs of our aged people. It is possible that some of these people have never been and are not now physically handicapped. There is a great gap in our social security program and especially for those people who are handicapped, who will never be able to work and who have no hope for the future as far as a cure of their disability is concerned. I plead with the government that, since this resolution is before the house once again, we close this gap and that physically and mentally handicapped people be given an opportunity for better care.
This resolution has always met with the approval of the house on previous occasions. I have never heard one hon. member dissent from it and say that he was not in favour of it, but invariably it has been talked out. We should have a statement from the minister today telling us where he stands on this


matter, and whether he is prepared to give these deserving people a pension and to take them into the welfare group.

Mr. Speaker, I want to support this resolution. I cannot discuss it from a legal point of view nor from the medical point of view. I can discuss it only as a dirt farmer. I know it would be a tremendous benefit to many people in this country who are unable to earn their own living. On many occasions we have had representations from different organizations who have spoken for people who were unable to earn their own livelihood. We know of men and women who have had children who have never grown up. They have been a drain on their parents during the whole of their lives. When the old folks get up in years their greatest concern is, what is going to happen to their offspring who have not been able to look after themselves. As I understand this resolution, it would take care of these poor people.
Then we have a group of people between the ages of fifty and sixty-five-mostly women, I think-who, when they reach that age, are worn out and are unable to provide for themselves. This resolution would take them in and do something for them. I know a lady in my constituency who has worked all the days of her life scrubbing floors in a large hotel, and doing that kind of work. During that time she has paid into the unemployment insurance fund. When she reached the age of fifty she was not able to get down on her knees to scrub floors. She applied for unemployment insurance. They said: "Well, have you lost your job?" She said, "No, I have not lost my job but I was sick and unable to work." They said, "We cannot do anything for you." I think this resolution would take care of people like that. It would provide them with something for a rainy day. I would hope that what would be paid would be not less than what an old age pensioner gets.
Then the question always comes up: Can we afford it? This government and previous governments have always found the money for anything worth while. I do not think there will be any trouble about that. If you explain to the people what a tax is for, if it is something legitimate and really needed you will have their support. So we would have no trouble getting taxes to pay for it.
The resolution deals to some extent with the federal and provincial governments. I hope that there will be no passing of the buck as there has been in other cases. When the act or the amendment to the act is brought in I hope that there will be no room for any misunderstanding and that these people will get this as of right.

I do not want to take up any more time this afternoon except to say that I am sure the rest of my group are behind me in supporting this resolution. I hope the minister will make a statement and tell us just how far he is prepared to go in making this resolution a reality, and that we can have a vote on it to see what is the view of the house. In my years here I have never found anyone who was against a resolution of this kind.

Mr. Speaker, my colleagues and I consider this resolution to be one of extreme importance. We welcome an opportunity of again expressing our views. On previous occasions we have sponsored similar resolutions and have brought forward the matter time and time again during debate. I repeat, we welcome this opportunity of offering our unanimous support.
The hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) is to be commended for having sponsored the resolution. Because he is an esteemed and conscientious member of this house, because he is a Liberal member of this house, we trust that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) already has sent word forth among Liberal members to give this resolution their unqualified support.
I well recall that when we served on the old age security committee in 1950 this matter kept coming forward time and time again. While we were not authorized under the terms of reference to deal specifically with the handicapped, we found it virtually impossible to keep a consideration of these persons out of the committee. I am quite confident that when we submitted our findings to this house we had them in mind. I should like to refer to finding No. 9, reported on page 101 of the report of the joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons on old age security. Speaking of premature ageing and invalidity the committee asserted:
The reverse of the problem of retaining older workers in the labour market is that presented by the prematurely aged and invalids who are obliged to retire from employment before their normal time. The committee has been deeply impressed by the evidence presented as to the position in which invalids and incurables find themselves at present. It has also received representations from organizations representing the blind, and blindness is, of course, part of the total problem of invalidity. The committee has felt, however, that the terms of reference established for it ruled out the possibility of a detailed examination of this problem as it applies to the younger age group.
Finding No. 23 is reported on page 103 of the report. This is headed "Other Claims to Priority" and reads:
Finally, in its study of the old age security systems in effect in other countries, and in its
Pensions for Disabled Persons consideration of the evidence presented by representative Canadian organizations and individuals, the committee has had to keep constantly in mind the place of old age in an over-all social security program. While the terms of reference of the committee have limited its study to the specific field of old age security, it has not felt it advisable to overlook the fact that there are other areas of social need in which governments, both provincial and federal, may be called upon to take in the future a substantial measure of responsibility.
I repeat that time and time again during the deliberations of that committee we heard from members representing all parties in the committee that the time had come when something specific and concrete should be done for persons who are incapacitated and as a consequence unable to provide for themselves.
The national advisory committee on the rehabilitation of the disabled estimates that there are approximately 150,000 people in Canada of working age who are victims of accident and disabling illnesses, including mental illnesses and so forth, and who are in dire need of support. I am not unmindful of the fact that some action has been taken toward providing rehabilitation services. Possibly I could go so far as to say that considerable action has been taken with respect to that one aspect of the problem. In looking over the report of the Department of National Health and Welfare for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1951, I notice that reference is made to the fact that during the course of the year activities in the field of rehabilitation were directed primarily towards preparations for the national conference on the rehabilitation of disabled persons which took place in Toronto during the first three days of February, 1951. Let us not forget that that is almost two years ago. It states here that the conference was scheduled originally to take place during May in the previous year but was postponed for certain very good reasons.
I notice in the report that the conference, which carried on its deliberations through two working committees, one dealing with vocational guidance, training and placement of handicapped persons and the other with the medical aspects of rehabilitation, approved a large number of resolutions. It recommended that the federal government appoint a full-time co-ordinator of rehabilitation activities in Canada and that a national advisory committee be established to co-ordinate the work of rehabilitation planning.
I noted when examining a recent issue of the Labour Gazette that reference was made to this problem of rehabilitation. On page 1566 of the December, 1952, issue of the Labour Gazette, under the heading "National Plan for Rehabilitation of Civilian Handicapped

Pensions for Disabled Persons being Drafted", it is stated that the national advisory committee would hold another meeting in September of 1952. I was deeply interested in the reported comments of some of those who are members of the national advisory committee. Dr. G. Fred McNally, who is chairman of the committee, stated that the period of broad examination of the problem was over. Once again I should like to emphasize that he said that the period of broad examination was over and that the time had come for positive action on specific objectives. To quote his exact words, he said:
The committee must live up to the expectations of thousands of Canadians, physically handicapped and unable to work, who look hopefully to it for efforts which will ultimately help them to a full, useful and productive life.
I also notice that Mr. Ian Campbell, national co-ordinator of rehabilitation, said, speaking of his trips to various provinces of Canada:
Wherever I went people, working with the handicapped, appeared to be encouraged by the fact that we now have a national headquarters for rehabilitation, and that the government of Canada has taken action in this field.
I stated earlier that I wanted to emphasize the fact that I fully realized that work, effective work I believe, has been going on for two years in the field of rehabilitation. Before I leave this point may I add that Mr. Campbell, in speaking of the objectives, asserted:
__money is not spent on the rehabilitation of the
handicapped. It is invested in their future.
I think that is absolutely correct. He says:
Who can doubt the wisdom of a program that makes the dependent independent, makes the nonproducer a producer and makes consumers of wealth creators of wealth?
I stated that was my last reference but I find that I desire to make one more. I wish to refer to three resolutions adopted by the committee last September. Here is the first one:
A broadening of the Canadian vocational training scheme so that handicapped persons may obtain academic and pre-vocational training needed for specific employment.
I am going to inquire of the minister exactly what action has been taken up to the present time with respect to these resolutions. The first one to which I have made reference has to do with a broadening of the Canadian vocational training scheme so that handicapped persons may obtain the academic and pre-vocational training needed for specific employment. I should like to know what has been done. After all, these recommendations were made last September. Here is the second one:
Organization of the rehabilitation program at the provincial level but with federal grants for such aspects as medical care, training and placement.


We are vitally concerned about this matter and I think the minister should indicate to us whether anything has been done with respect to that resolution. In the third place they made the following recommendation:
A "pilot" survey on the physically handicapped now registered for work with the national employment service in Montreal.
Possibly the minister could indicate in the course of his observations whether that survey has been made or is under way. If it has been completed, then I believe the results should be made known to us. I certainly desire to commend the national advisory committee for the work which I know they have done in this field. I also wish to commend the Department of National Health and Welfare and the minister and his officers for what has been done in this respect. I hope that the minister is able to report progress in keeping with the spirit which I am told prevailed throughout the meetings of the national advisory committee.
That deals with one aspect of the problem only, the rehabilitation of those who are capable of rehabilitation, but it does not solve the whole problem by any stretch of the imagination. I stated a moment ago that, according to the advisory committee, there are 150,000 people of working age in Canada who are, using the broad general term, incapacitated. Let us not delude ourselves into believing that, because the report speaks of them as being of working age, they are capable of working. I do not know what percentage of this group would be incapable of working. Only a comprehensive survey would provide that answer.
I should also like to know if any information has been procured with respect to the number of persons who may be incapacitated but who cannot be included within that group of working age, which I presume may be from 16 to 60 years of age. We have that other group of wholly incapacitated persons. I am not so concerned about the difficulty, if there is one, in ascertaining the degree of incapacitation because I know that so far as veterans are concerned under the Pension Act there is a medical board with a competent medical staff, and they are presumed to be in a position to ascertain whether a man is suffering from a 10 per cent disability or 100 per cent disability. I cannot see why a similar committee, board, oi; whatever you want to call it, staffed with competent medical men, cannot do just as competent a job with respect to our incapacitated people.
I realize that certain incapacitated persons have been taken care of. I realize fully that when the old age security measure was introduced we brought into that group certain

incapacitated persons. I realize that we brought a great many incapacitated persons into the Old Age Assistance Act. As indicated by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), I realize fully that in some instances widows' pensions are provided under mothers' allowances acts and that under other measures we have taken care of a number of them. However, I have to take issue mildly with him so far as taking care of them under unemployment insurance is concerned, because my understanding is that once you become physically incapacitated you can qualify for no benefits whatsoever. I think that was just a slip on the part of the hon. member for Lanark.
We feel that at this particular time, Mr. Speaker, two years after the national advisory committee had its first meeting, and possibly many years after the Department of National Health and Welfare began to look into this matter, we should have a fairly comprehensive and up-to-date report from the minister during the discussion of this resolution. We have in Canada an association of incurables. I want to pay my tribute to the executive members of that association, and particularly to Miss Eva Warden, who took the initiative in organizing these persons into an association. To those of us who saw them here a couple of years ago, most of them in wheelchairs, it was a pathetic sight. They were not asking for charity. They were asking for a place in our general field of social welfare. They were asking for an opportunity for those possessed of any physical or mental ability to be able to engage in productive enterprises.
I realize fully the importance of that field, but in discussing the matter with them I have also come to realize that they recognize that there is one very serious problem that must be taken care of right now, the problem of those who are wholly incapacitated. I know that representatives of the association of incurables have met the minister. They have indicated to me that he has always given them a very courteous reception but their efforts have not always culminated in the end result for which they were hoping. However, I think he gave them courage and hope. Of course the minister is capable of doing that without too much effort. Nevertheless I still have a good deal of confidence that it will not be too long before their wishes will be fully realized. I do not know whether or not they have seen the minister recently. If not, conceivably they have arranged to see him. I have the idea that they probably will. I have before me their resolution, which I shall not read, but it indicates clearly and definitely that they feel 68108-63
Pensions for Disabled Persons that pensions are a most necessary part of whatever general program is adopted to take care of the problem of the incurable.
I am going to take my lead from the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). I realize fully that one could talk on and on with respect to a matter of this kind, but let me conclude with this one observation, that, while I know that we should soon be giving consideration to certain amendments to the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act, I am conscientiously of the opinion that before we do more in those particular fields-where we have at least done something for those people-we should do something for those incurables. That is particularly so for those who are incapable of earning a living.
Now, I do not want that statement to be misconstrued. I am not wholly satisfied with all aspects of our old age security program or our old age assistance program, but I do feel that if we are going to move forward at all with respect to social welfare we should move in this direction and make some provision for these people-so that we can thus bring into their lives some ray of hope. They have waited a long time. They have been patient-and I think the minister will confirm that statement. While I did not sit in on any of their conferences with him, I dare say they were modest in the form of their presentations before him. I trust that before too long they will be able to say that the minister in the past has demonstrated his concern and brought results in other fields of social welfare and has now done the same thing for them.

Mr. Speaker, I agree completely with the principle expressed in this resolution, which is to pay a $40 a month pension to all people who, through disability, are no longer able to earn their own living. After all, it is exactly the same principle as that embodied in the Old Age Security Act, which assumes that when a person reaches the age of 70 they are no longer able to earn their own living and are, therefore, entitled to a pension.
Now, if a person has a disability which cannot be cured, and if that incurable disability is such that the person cannot be taught a trade which will enable him to continue to earn his own living and provide for his family, then I firmly believe that person should be assisted by the government in the form of a pension.
However, I believe that the very first thing to do is to try to cure that disability, and, failing that, to try to teach that person a
994	HOUSE OF
Pensions for Disabled Persons trade. This will require a well planned and well carried out rehabilitation program, both physical and occupational.
Now, an example of a physical rehabilitation case is that of a man who is only suited to do heavy manual work and who develops a bad hernia. If the hernia is not cured, the man is prevented from continuing to earn his living, and he simply has to remain in idleness. However, if it is made possible for that man to have an operation for that hernia and it can be cured, he can continue to earn his own living.
An example of an occupational rehabilitation case is where a man loses his sight. In a great many cases that man can be taught to handle his old job by the use of guards and aids supplied to him by the Canadian National Institute for the Blind. If that is impossible owing to the nature of his old job, then the great likelihood is that he can be taught a new trade. That sort of thing is going on all the time where opportunities are provided for the Canadian National Institute for the Blind to step in and carry out their very excellent work.
Those are only two examples of what can be done to make it possible for those who have become incapacitated, by accident or disease, to continue to earn their own living. I am firmly convinced that no worth-while person wants charity or to continue in idleness. What they do want is to be able to continue to earn their own living and to retain their independence. I believe that a well planned and well executed rehabilitation program, worked out in co-operation with the provinces, will, in the great majority of cases, make this a reality.
It is well known to all of us that at the end of the last war a very great number of disabled veterans were either taught a new trade or taught how to continue with their old trade despite their disability. I believe that if this same kind of program is carried on on the same kind of scale throughout Canada, a great many more people in industry would be able to continue to earn their own living than is today the case.
I believe it is the responsibility of the federal government to work out with the provinces such a rehabilitation program, and I very much hope that the rehabilitation committee, which has been in operation now for a year, is steadily working toward that end. Like the member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw), I am looking forward very much to hearing a report from the minister today on the progress of that committee.
I believe that a rehabilitation program such as I have outlined would ensure that


all disabled persons would have the right, which I believe should be the right of every citizen of this country, to have the opportunity to cure their disability and, failing that, to learn a trade by which they can continue to earn their own living and remain independent. In cases where that is absolutely impossible, I believe that the government should ipay those people a disability pension equal to the old age pension.
As the member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) pointed out this afternoon, the Ontario government has given a very good lead in matters of that kind. Since the first of January of last year, they have been paying a disability pension of $40 a month to disabled people. This has provided very much needed relief to a large number of disabled people, and I believe that is the kind of thing we should aim at here in this parliament. I believe that the federal government should co-operate with the provinces and make this kind of pension available to all permanently disabled Canadians.
I earnestly urge the minister to see that steps are taken to make this a reality at the earliest possible opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I wish at this time to congratulate the member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) on bringing in this resolution. We have both worked towards bringing in a resolution of this kind for some considerable time. I believe the last time I spoke on a resolution similar to this was on March 7 last. I also spoke about this in the year before.
I would like to have the resolution which I have on the order paper coupled with this resolution, Mr. Speaker, so that it will save the time of the house. My resolution reads: That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into early consideration the advisability of including in their social security program the payment of pensions or maintenance allowances, equal and similar to blind pensions, for the unfortunate crippled people of Canada.
If these two resolutions are coupled I am sure they will be considered by the government. Whatever decision the government makes will be influenced by the way in which the parties of this house agree to such legislation.
In this day and age, when there are pensions for people who are not nearly as deserving as these unfortunates, I think the time has come when we will have to do something. Having been nearer (to the people than I am here in the House of Commons, having been the reeve of a municipality for some ten years, I have had the opportunity of going into many homes where people were

not able to earn a dollar for themselves. I certainly realize the stresses and strains which can be put on families who have to depend on the allowance given out by rural municipalities. The municipalities have to depend for their revenue on land taxes, and in these times the municipalities are finding it very difficult to obtain additional revenue for things of this kind.
I represent seven different municipalities in the constituency of Springfield, and there are approximately five of these cases in every municipality. Since there are about 175 municipalities in Manitoba, this would mean that some 875 people would be benefited by such legislation. The municipalities would benefit also in not being charged for this relief. There is no doubt but that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has gone a very long way in bringing help to many people in Canada, but I believe this is also a problem which the dominion should handle. It is something that should be thoroughly considered. The dominion government takes full responsibility for the returned soldiers, and I am sure that when this problem is thoroughly considered it will be found that these unfortunate people should not be the care of the province but should be the responsibility of the dominion.
We are asked where the money will come from. A few years ago people thought that the introduction of family allowances would break the country. Since that time it has been found that these allowances stimulate buying power. I believe that money for this purpose can be found in the same way as it was found for family allowances. If cheques were issued to these needy people by the dominion government, it would create buying power for others who have the capacity to produce.
Like the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor), I do not wish to speak at length on this matter. I want to see this motion come to a vote. I hope the other members in the house will see fit to terminate their speeches before six o'clock so that a vote can be taken.

I am not going to speak at any length either, Mr. Speaker. I believe most of the members of this house who have had any experience in the municipalities realize the necessity for the legislation proposed in this resolution. The resolution asks for a pension for incapacitated people, and I am not going to couple the question of rehabilitation of the handicapped with it because I think that is a separate problem. I am glad the resolution has been moved by a government member. I believe the last time it was before the house 68108-631
Pensions for Disabled Persons it was moved by a government member. Apparently they have done some thinking about it in the last few years; at least they should have. I am disappointed in the fact that nothing has been done other than think about it. There has been no legislation, and no indication of legislation.
So far as the minister is concerned, I am reasonably sure of his opinion on this matter. I am sure also that he has not been able to persuade the treasury board, or something like this would have been provided along with old age security. This particular type of legislation, Mr. Speaker, would fill in the gaps in our social security program. There is a very wide gap there, and perhaps the most pathetic sight in our country is the people who would benefit by this legislation. In my own riding I have about 84,000 people. The constituency covers an area of about 14 miles, and when I am at home I sit in the middle of it. I see a great many people who would come within the provisions of such legislation as is proposed here. It is a sad sight, and it is difficult to have to tell most of these people, when they come to talk to you about their problem, that the only relief provided is by the municipality.
I am thinking particularly at this time of the women in the age group 50 to 65. There is a fifteen-year gap there. I am thinking of the women who raised families and contributed sons and grandsons to the armed services. The average woman living in a home on an average income has had a rather tough life. While she may not be a paraplegic, as defined by the medical people, she is incapacitated to the extent that she has broken down prematurely under the pressure of maintaining a home on an inadequate income. Such people finish up without even a home; with no income and requiring medical attention. These people are not being helped by the provincial government either. There is no provincial legislation under which they can be helped. I have placed hundreds of cases in the hands of the provincial welfare department, only to be told that there was no provincial legislation under which these people could be helped. They become a charge on the bankrupt municipalities. Most of the municipalities across this country are bankrupt, or very nearly bankrupt. It is there that these people must seek relief, and there is no relief there for them.
Think of an old lady between 60 and 65 who comes in and tells you her pathetic story. She has no home, and has been living with friends and neighbours. Some of them are diabetics and require insulin every day, which is a costly process. Then we have to

Pensions for Disabled Persons tell them that there is no relief provincially; there is none nationally, so they have to go over to the relief committee of the municipality. When they go there they are told, "We have not the funds to care for you." It is nearly time we reached the point of doing something about it.
Then there is the case of the paraplegic, the person who is permanently crippled. Many of them are born that way, and many are crippled by injury or the lack of medical attention. A while ago there was a pilgrimage here, and I am sure all members recall the gallery full of wheelchairs that we had exhibited in order to emphasize the necessity of doing something for these people. Many of these people sit alone in lonesome silence. Others have the problem of raising funds for the care of chronic illnesses and diseases, and some are being supported by recipients of the old age security pension. There is a considerable burden there.
I believe the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Shaw) placed the number of these people at 150,000. Perhaps quite a number could be weeded out if you followed a definition of "incapacitated". There would not be very much money involved. I believe the government should, at this time, consider doing something for them. Now, the government may not want to pass a national pension act or make money available to the provinces, in view of the fact that this is a municipal responsibility. From a provincial standpoint, Ontario is doing something about the matter, as is Saskatchewan, so we would not have those provinces to contend with. I think Alberta does something, too. If the minister would take under consideration the problem of checking with the municipalities across the country as to the number of incapacitated people they have who would be affected by this kind of legislation, and making grants in aid to the municipalities to supplement their income, so the matter could be administered from there, I think it would be a good thing. As to a municipality that could take care of itself, you would not have to help it. But if, instead of making a grant in aid of that kind to the province, which involves more administrative cost, it was given to the municipality where it could be handled directly, in my opinion you would save a great deal of money that would be wasted in administration if it went to the province. I think something like that could be done for immediate relief without raising the whole question of another pension.
But I think the final answer to the thing is this. What Canada needs is an over-all social security act. With the piecemeal legislation that we have now, including old age
IMr. Gillls.l

assistance by the provinces, pensions to the incapacitated in Ontario and some of the other provinces; with the millions of dollars that are collected by charitable organizations across this country for the purpose of supposedly helping people of this type, in my opinion the money wasted in administration and in the duplication of machinery would more than pay for a pension to people in this category. I think the government has got to get around fairly soon to the establishment of an over-all social security act whereby you can take in your old age pensioners, your old age assistance recipients and your incapacitated people, and buttress all that with an over-all health program. Definitely the biggest item in this type of legislation is the medical cost which has to be borne by these people without any income. I believe an over-all act administered by the national government and handled from here would have the effect of cutting the administration cost you have now across this country in duplicated services. I think you would save enough money to pay for this pension by tidying up all your social security measures in one over-all act.
I know the minister is just straining at the leash to get to his feet and tell us that his department has given this matter a great deal of consideration and that within the foreseeable future the necessary legislation will be brought down to take care of this particular problem.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to take up much time. I am anxious that this resolution come to a vote and am still more anxious that it become legislation as soon as possible. I happen to have three cases in my own village in which, as a result of the act that is now in force in the province of Ontario, these people have been taken off the relief rolls of a burdened municipality. I think the same thing will apply in many cases across the Dominion of Canada. Every one of us knows that our municipalities are burdened with taxes they can hardly bear; they cannot stand any more.
This is necessary legislation, and it is going to take some of the weight off the municipalities as well as being of benefit to those who will receive assistance. For instance, a totally disabled person is bound to be on the relief rolls in 90 per cent of the cases. In my municipality in the province of Ontario they receive approximately $4 a week. That is a meagre handout to anybody who is on his back and unable to work and earn a living. I see that the resolution suggests a pension equal to the old age pension

so this legislation, if it came in, would provide a pension of approximately $40 a month. That would be a grand idea. It would be a grand help to those in need. I thank you for the opportunity of making these few remarks.

Mr. Speaker, I think everything that can be said in support of this resolution has been said, and I am glad that everything that has been said has been in support of it. I should simply like to endorse what has been said and to register my support also. I am impelled to do that by representations which have been made to me by individuals and by organizations, and indeed by my own inclinations. I think we have long passed the day of the doctrine of the survival of the fittest with regard to the care of these incapacitated people. As to those who are blind, we have assumed our responsibility although I think perhaps we have not gone far enough yet. The abolition of the means test with regard to pensions for the blind would seem to be the next logical step that we might take.
We have seen members of an organization of incapacitated or incurable people. You will probably remember, Mr. Speaker, that we had them with us here some time ago. A year or two ago they came to see us in our offices. At that time I was impressed by the lightness of spirit and the brilliance of mind displayed by many of these people. They are capable of some constructive and useful work. As a matter of fact, many are doing some now. But to ask them to compete in the open labour market of the country is simply cruel and inhuman.
In the days of my youth such people were the recipients of private charity. They were looked after by their relations as best those relations could afford to do that duty or else -which was a good deal worse-they were the recipients of public charity. In that type of charity it is certainly more blessed to give than to receive. When we occupy ourselves in charity we have a feeling of virtue which is its own reward and a certain warmth around the heart from the knowledge that we can help others less fortunate than ourselves.
But I suggest that it is often difficult for the recipients of either form of the charity which I have mentioned. I would suggest that we might give ourselves collectively as a nation, rather than individually, that warm feeling I have mentioned, and at the same time give to these people not only sustenance of their bodies which is needful to them but also something which in my opinion is just
Pensions for Disabled Persons as important, namely a spirit of independence of mind, so they would feel that they have some dignity and some right to live and to enjoy, to some extent at least, those things which are enjoyed by people physically more fortunate than themselves.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to take up much time in speaking on this resolution; but having spoken on behalf of the incapacitated at each session from 1945 down to the present time, I wished to say a few words at this time. My purpose in rising is to endorse the principle of this resolution and to say to the minister, on behalf of the people I have the honour to represent, that they are looking to him now to bring in the legislation he considers to be necessary to carry into effect the request contained in this resolution.
That is all I have to say at the present time. We have listened to some excellent speeches on this matter not only today but in former years. I want to commend the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) for introducing this resolution. I also wish to say that the learned doctor, the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair), has given us the medical side of it in language we can all understand.

As one
who has been privileged to enjoy the very best of health during my lifetime, I want to give my wholehearted support to the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). I have spoken on this matter on a number of occasions during the past four or five years. We have been put off the beam a little bit by the statement of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) that a survey was being made by the provinces in order to deal with this matter. I believe the survey has been completed, and we expect action at this session and no later.
Having spoken of my own good health and looking back over the years since I have been here, like many others I realize that because of conditions imposed upon me I have great difficulty in making a living for myself and my family. Having that in mind, I can realize very clearly the position in which these people who are physically handicapped find themselves, and also the position in which many of the people who are responsible for those incapacitated persons find themselves when they are unable to do very much for those unfortunate ones.
I feel that this legislation should be enacted during this session. I understand that a committee from the organization for the blind interviewed the Minister of National Health

Pensions for Disabled Persons and Welfare today. They asked for two things in particular, namely increasing the pension from $40 to $50 a month and removing the means test. I hope the minister will take cognizance of the representations that have been made to him and that he will see to it that this request is granted, and that before this session concludes, that is, that before we have another election he will get down to business and see that pensions at least equal to old age pensions are provided for those physically incapacitated.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. J. Browne (St. John's West):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I notice that the proposer of this resolution speaks of the advisability of cooperating with the provincial governments. We have been informed here this afternoon that Ontario has an act which provides pensions for incapacitated persons, and I believe that similar legislation exists in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. It gives me great pleasure this afternoon to draw to the attention of hon. members the fact that in Newfoundland we have legislation dealing with this very subject. It was passed in December, 1949, nine months after the province came into confederation. Under that act a monthly allowance may be paid out of funds provided by the government-
-to adults or families who through mental or physical incapacity or other exigency are unable to provide in whole or in part by their own efforts or from income or other resources necessities essential to maintain or assist in maintaining a reasonably normal and healthy existence.
Incapacity is defined as-
-a condition of physical or mental illness or disability of such a nature as to render a person incapable of maintaining himself or his family and from which there is no reasonable prospect of recovery within a period of three months from the date of application for an allowance.
I am sure hon. members are familiar with cases of incapacitated persons, fathers or heads of families, who come to them and detail their sad circumstances. If there is no legislation of that kind on the statute books of the province, or if some provision is not made by the municipality, the situation is very desperate indeed. During the last couple of weeks, and especially during Christmas time, people came to me who had not gone through the right channels, and I was able to assist them and put them on the right track. They were not aware of this provision. I was able to assist them to get consideration from the dependents' allowances board, and they will get the pension during their incapacity.
My reason for taking part in this debate was chiefly to draw the attention of the house to the fact that Newfoundland, which is the youngest province, has legislation of this kind. At the same time I feel it is not

fair that a province-and this applies to all provinces except the two major ones-that has not the sources of revenue that the central government has, should have to bear this burden. The resolution refers to co-operating with the provinces. It seems to me that the funds to meet this liability should be provided by the central government.
I should not like to see any further extension of the power of the central government in regard to the examination of persons as to their qualifications for such an allowance or pension. I feel that it should be done by leaving the matter in the hands of the provinces with the central government providing the money.

Mr. Speaker, like other members of the C.C.F. group I believe that the long-term solution of this problem lies in an over-all national health program. Nevertheless I am quite ready to support the measure before us, even though it be piecemeal legislation. After all, I suppose, one cannot expect those who support the Liberal party and the Liberal government to be Liberals in a hurry. They tell us that the Liberals who are in a hurry sit in this corner of the house.
Why do you speak like that?
The Prime Minister said that at one time.

I would suggest, Mr. Speaker, that we are making progress even though we are still under a Liberal government. There is a very excellent committee under the auspices of the minister's department known as the national advisory committee on the rehabilitation of the disabled, which is apparently getting down to the job of helping these people, helping them in the way of securing treatment to regain their health to the point where they can assist themselves, and also helping them in the matter of retraining. If one can judge by the recommendations which were passed at the last meeting of that committee one may conclude that it is on the road toward doing a reasonably good job. But notwithstanding all that is being done, there are still some very large gaps in our social security program, large gaps pertaining to these incurables.
In the first place, I can find no reliable estimate of just how many such people we have in this country, how many unemployable incurables there are in Canada. The bureau of statistics tell me that they are unable to find any estimate, and no effort has been made to acquire any accurate estimate of the number of these unemployable incurables. I notice that the Canadian association of the

incurables estimates that there are probably 48,000 unemployable incurables in the province of Ontario alone. I have no idea just how close that comes to the truth, but certainly the time has come when we should at least find out how many of these people there are in Canada. It would seem that we have not been too considerate of these people, in that we have not even tried to find out how many there are needing such assistance.	*
As has been pointed out already, at the last session of its legislature the province of Ontario introduced legislation to assist disabled persons. But here again is an example of how stupid government legislation can be. That act could do a good job with the minister in charge being in full sympathy with its provisions, but the regulations are that to be eligible to receive assistance under the act one must be both permanently and totally disabled. I have people in my riding who have been certified by the medical committee of the provincial department of public welfare to be permanently disabled, but because they can still dress themselves if given enough time and can struggle from one room in their house to another without having to be carried, they are not considered to be eligible for help under that act.
I am sorry the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) is not present today, because one case has been brought to my attention which has been before the Department of Veterans Affairs and the provincial department of public welfare. This is an air force man 33 years of age, who had served four years and eight months in the air force. He is a victim of what the medical authorities call progressive muscular dystrophy. This means that he is gradually losing the use of all his muscles. He has not been able to work for over two years.
The Department of Veterans Affairs say that this disease is not the result of his service, that it was not brought on because of conditions experienced during service. The man states that while in the service he felt his hands becoming numb but did not report that to the medical officer. Therefore he receives no assistance or consideration from the Department of Veterans Affairs. The provincial department of public welfare cannot help him under the new act. While he is permanently disabled, while there is no known cure for his condition and no likelihood of his being able to work again, he is not considered to be totally disabled because he can walk to the toilet himself without having to be carried.
This simply illustrates how stupid some government legislation can be when it sets
Pensions for Disabled Persons out to help people. I suggest that any action which is taken to help these unfortunate people should provide for more generous regulations than those laid down by the government of Ontario in their new act. The time has certainly come when we should provide for those who cannot be cured or rehabilitated, and who must depend for support either upon relatives or the public generally. I sincerely support the measure before the house and hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will be able to prevail upon his colleagues on the treasury benches to give the kind of help we are asking this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, it is not necessary to repeat the things which have been said already in support of this measure. I desire merely to make it known that I am heartily in support of this resolution and will vote for it. I think the case of Social Credit has been put forward quite adequately by former speakers.
I wish merely to point out that there is no conceivable reason why the implementation of what is called for in this resolution should entail any increased taxation. I believe at the present time this country is carrying as great a taxation burden as it should be called upon to carry. I submit that our ability to provide assistance such as is envisaged in this resolution should depend upon our ability to produce goods and services. Certainly no other view could be realistic.
The production of Canada in 1952 has been estimated at between $22 billion and $23 billion worth of goods and services. Surely it ought to be possible to provide the rather meagre assistance suggested by this resolution without adding to our taxation burden. With our production as great is it is, if we must increase our taxation in order to provide this amount of assistance to our people then it is clear that our financial system is unrealistic. We should therefore examine the possibility of learning how to do more of what is physically possible, by a reformation of our financial system.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to commend the hon. gentleman for bringing in this resolution. This is typical of the sort of thing he does in this house. His heart is all-out for people who are underprivileged and need assistance. This resolution is meant to assist a group of people in this country who greatly need assistance.
I agree with the hon. member that the work of the Minister of National Health and

Pensions for Disabled Persons Welfare (Mr. Martin) at the United Nations has been a great credit to himself and to Canada. We were all pleased to observe the manner in which he stood up against the delegates from Russia and other communist countries, how he engaged in debate with them and with his most courteous and able manner was able to hold his own and warrant the commendation of the press of the United States, certainly of this country, and of Great Britain and other countries.
What has this to do with the resolution?

It has a lot to do
with it, because the voice of Canada was heard at the United Nations. The world was learning that Canada is a great and humane nation, and that in offering leadership to the rest of the world she was prepared to put her own house in good shape. You know what Robert Burns said, that if each before his ain door swept, the village would be clean. If by passing legislation such as is proposed in this resolution we show that in every sense we are a Christian nation, we will then be able to present a better claim for leadership before the world at the United Nations or any other conference or world parliament.
I want to say at the same time that taxation is very high in this country, and that there will be an unwillingness to add to that taxation; but the implementation of this resolution would not necessarily add very much to the amount of taxes the average person would pay. Canada has shown a very good example to the world in its care for aged people, its old age pension legislation, its mothers' allowances and the work that is being done in the field of health and welfare and hospitalization.
Turning from these matters, great work has been done in the field of labour through the abolition of child labour, the limiting of hours of work, improvement of conditions for workers, the introduction of the eight-hour day, and more recently the approach to the five-day week. As I have said before in the house, there is a possibility that we can travel too rapidly along these lines inasmuch as so many countries in the world do not have that sort of advanced legislation.
As we know, half our revenues today are being spent on defence to maintain armies and make ourselves strong together with our allies. Our men are in Korea and on the continent of Europe. They are learning that other countries on the face of the earth are not as well off as Canada and that other


countries face real problems in even maintaining a bare existence, let alone having the type of advanced legislation that we have in Canada.
So far as the old age measure is concerned, I believe an amendment should be introduced to permit pensioners to earn money in excess of their pension. I think it is a harsh thing to prevent these people from earning any money. In my opinion men of advancing years can offer great service to every community. I do not say that they should be engaged in industry generally, but I think our legislation could be amended in order to allow a man receiving the old age pension to work in any kind of industry which does not call for the use of machinery and power equipment of that kind. Masonry is a lost art in this country, and there are men of years who are skilled in this craft. They know how to take a rough rock, break it and make a beautiful wall, arch or doorway. There are others who know the mysteries of gardening and are skilled in landscape gardening. Why not permit them to enter into work of that kind? Let them engage in carving, woodwork and any kind of handicraft where machinery is not used.
Men of intelligence and advanced years know the beauties of the landscape. They understand the planting of trees and things of that kind. Why not employ such men in the forests to thin out underbrush, plant new trees and thus add to the wealth of our country? Many of them are men of art who are skilled in sculpture or music. Why not permit them to engage to the full limit of their ability in these occupations and thus add to their own income and certainly to the beauty and comfort of those about them? They would set a good example for the young people who are coming along. Many of our young people are so mechanically minded and so attached to the machine age that they are losing touch with the crafts, skills and arts that are so essential in any country.
By releasing men of advanced age to carry on such work we would be adding to the wealth of our country and certainly to its beauty. Then there is the field of invention. If an old man has skill in a certain line and has an inventive mind, why should he not be encouraged to pursue that hobby and gain any advantage he can derive from such inventions, the proceeds of which should be credited to him and not deducted from his pension? The same thing applies to women, who are so often skilled in the arts of needlecraft, weaving, the dyeing of textiles, household management, and so on. I think it would be a forward step.

People might very well go to the province of Quebec and study some of the homecrafts that are flourishing there. I had the opportunity of spending some time in that province not long ago, and of visiting some of the farmhouses. I admired the beautiful works of the hands of artistic people in carving, woodwork, the manufacture of household furniture, etc., all of which added to the beauty and delight of living in the rural communities of Quebec. I am ashamed to admit that I had to wait until now before visiting the province of Quebec. While I was there I was struck with the fact that a very prosperous civilization has existed there for all these centuries based upon land which, in the west and in Ontario where I was born, in very many cases would not be considered worth cultivating. It seemed to me that we really do not have to have fertile land and a luxuriance of natural production in order to have a strong and virile people. I was reminded of a story about Glengarry-
