Mr. Speaker, if I rise to take part in this debate it is to reaffirm what I have said before in this house. In 1949, when taking part in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne I said this, and I am quoting from Hansard of September 16, page 19:
To increase social security, I would suggest to the government, if I may, that, in so far as our financial means allow, a pension plan be inaugurated for needy invalids. This would be looked upon favourably by the people of Canada.
Up to the present time, the government has provided for the blind, for the aged, for children; certain provinces grant pensions to needy mothers. The time has come to consider those poor unfortunates who, by accident or by birth, are crippled for life and gaze with sombre melancholy upon the happiness of others. A pension scheme designed to help them would ameliorate their plight. The kindness of the state would atone to some extent for the harshness of life.
There is no one more in favour of the resolution than I, and I would like to see it go through this chamber at the earliest possible time. When last I spoke in this house certain quarters seemed to put blame upon me because I spoke in English. I am glad to be able to say a few words in the course of our debates in the language of the majority of this house. I think that today is such an occasion when we must use the French language to ask the government of this country-all the governments of this country-to consider the unfortunate circumstances of those who have been incapacitated by some terrible accident or who were crippled at birth and are fated to remain so throughout their life.

Is their anything sadder than a visit to any of these charitable institutions where we find hundreds and thousands of human beings lying in pain, past expecting anything but what may come from Heaven, through their prayers, or from individual charity? The government of this country-all the governments of this country-must seek a solution to this problem, which is the problem of our sick and crippled people.
I admit that our latest old age pensions act takes care of approximately one-third of these unfortunate people. There still remain two-thirds comprising, so I am told, roughly between 50,000 and 60,000 persons awaiting government aid, that is aid from all the governments of this country.
They read in the newspapers and learn through the news and radio, besides being told by their relatives, that family allowances are being paid, that old age pensions are being given without a means test to all people 70 years of age, and that old age pensions are even granted to those who are 65 years of age. And they sadly ask themselves: When will our turn come?
I wish to congratulate the sponsor of this resolution. I also wish to congratulate him for having introduced such a resolution after the measures we have adopted in order to settle once and for all the case of our fellow citizens who are 70 years of age and more. This draft resolution is timely and necessary and all persons of good will in this house must rally behind the hon. member who has introduced it in order that this bill may become the law of the country.
However, in reading the notice of motion, I note that we are asked to consider:
-the advisability of co-operating with the provincial governments for the purpose of providing pensions, equal to old age pensions, for all those who are incapacitated and unable to earn their living, regardless of age.
It appears from the context of this resolution that the federal government cannot intervene, in spite of all its eagerness to do so, without obtaining first the co-operation of the provinces.
I remember that when family allowances were discussed in a certain province, it was argued in the legislature of that province that the legislation which the House of Commons intended to adopt in regard to family allowances was unconstitutional because it violated that section of the constitution which gives to the provinces the exclusive right of legislating in matters pertaining to education.

I understand that the enacting of legislation to assist incapacitated people would have no such scope. Still we must admit that it is impossible to arrive at practical conclusions without the co-operation of the provinces. There is nothing though to prevent us, the members of the House of Commons, from acting in such a way as to enlist the co-operation of the provinces in order to solve, once and for all, the problem of those unfortunate people who, languishing in hospital or staying with their families, often shed tears over their plight. There is something here that goes beyond a duty of public charity. We have adopted pension systems with a view to assisting those who were better off than these. We must look for a way, difficult though that may be, to make these unfortunate people-I hardly dare say the happiest people on earth, since we could never manage to do that-at least somewhat more comfortable, to alleviate their plight.
In conclusion I wish to thank the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) for the kind thoughts and pleasant words he has had for the province of Quebec. The people of that province are attached to their traditions, history and way of life, but they are never happier than when they are sure that our fellow citizens from the other provinces understand them.

By this time I believe we should all know that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has always been very sympathetic and open to conviction when any appeals of this sort have been made to him. There have been very few of them, if any, that have not been received graciously.
I noticed that none of the speakers who preceded me suggested just how much assistance might be given, other than is conveyed in the resolution which broadly states that some pension should be provided. No one has suggested how it might be administered other than as a pension; and no one, of course, has suggested the cost. The cost perhaps may be the least of these factors.

In this matter of helping the incapacitated, the Department of National Health and Welfare has for years been making a generous contribution through assistance to hospitals, particularly children's hospitals. We all know that if some of the damage suffered by children is remedied early in life, the young people can grow up to be useful citizens and support themselves. Personally, I know that the children's hospitals in Nova Scotia, particularly the one in Halifax, are grateful for the assistance given. It has only been by reason of this assistance that they have been able to continue their work.
Social security has become a very popular phrase in recent years, Mr. Speaker. In the numerous discussions of this topic, social insurance has received the major emphasis and is sometimes considered the only issue, yet the gaps in our social service must not be overlooked. In referring to other measures, we sometimes refer to the means test which has become rather unpopular in Canada and other countries. However, the comments on the means test are unrealistic and impractical. If we think of the needs of the people and the ways in which those needs can be met within our economy, we must accept the fact that a government assistance plan based on a means test is an essential. Public assistance is recognized by all to be necessary until other social security measures are more practically and more adequately developed. In any period in the foreseeable future it will continue to be necessary. There will always have to be provision for the residue of those in need and for those who, for various technical reasons, are not eligible for other assistance.
Since there are those for whom specific provision is not made under insurance and other schemes we must, whether we like it or not, include a means test program in our provisions for those in need. I would presume that was included, even though not mentioned, in the resolution. I believe that, to date, the program is twofold. How do we reduce the number to whom public assistance offers the only security in time of destitution or when they become incapacitated? How do we provide a public assistance program that will give some security, that will be a constructive measure for the person who is in need of its help, and which will be satisfactory to the community and those residing among us?
There are many different views about our planning for social security and welfare. Let us consider here only the significant ones. There are many constructive views about the administration of public assistance. At the present time the national revulsion to 68108-644
Pensions for Disabled Persons the means test is a reaction to destruction. This means test is supposed to be destructive to the person to whom it is applied. There is a difference in the attitude to the old age assistance and mothers' allowance programs as compared to the social assistance for the needy. These are all public assistance and government programs. What makes the difference in attitude? The administration is not better in the former than in the latter. The difference is largely in the public attitude towards the causes of illness. There is little or no stigma attached to the fact of being incapacitated. In our present economy, the difficulty of making adequate provision for such an eventuality is recognized by most of us. We therefore do not attach personal blame to the person who has not been able to provide adequately for a crippled member of his family.
The development of categories for assistance was probably necessary in the process of changing public attitudes. I hope the time will come when we can eliminate such categories; when our communities and provinces will be prepared to recognize a responsibility to people who are unable to provide themselves with the necessities of life; when public assistance will be given on proof of need, and the question of why the person is in need will not determine whether or not he or she receives help, although it will certainly influence the other constructive services which may be available.
How can we make a government assistance program constructive? Government assistance costs the people money. In its short-term planning a constructive program will cost more money than an inadequate one. Good legislation and good administration are dependent on the community, on the people's attitude to the problem, and upon their willingness, of course, to spend and to ensure that the program is good. The public attitude has also its effect upon the recipients, upon those who hesitate to apply, upon their selfrespect and their morale, upon their ability to recognize and perform their obligations as citizens, and upon their attitudes to themselves and to society.
We have come some distance from the time when the pauper was disqualified from all citizenship rights, although remnants of those old days still remain. But I am afraid we are still far from the point where destitution does not carry with it some element of personal disgrace, which makes it difficult for the destitute, crippled or incapacitated person, regardless of the cause of his condition, to remain a respected and contributing

In approaching this resolution and giving it consideration we should certainly change our thinking in that regard. This consideration forces us back to the reason the community has for establishing a public assistance program. Why does society give public assistance? And after all "society" really means government. The motives vary, and the nature of the program depends on those motives. I outline them here without attempting to assess their relative importance in different communities. We give to people in many instances when we see them almost reach the point of starvation. That is a grudging, negative attitude associated with our discomfort in the face of human suffering.
We must protect the incapacitated from the results of destitution. I think that is what the hon. member had in mind when this resolution was introduced. The effect may be upon their health, their safety, our personal income; that is yours and mine, for example. The result can be a loss to the property owner because a crippled person cannot pay rent; or it can have an effect upon the total economy in the loss of purchasing power and of manpower. The result may be in the ultimate cost in the increase of disease and crime because, as you are aware, an incapacitated person in many instances has an extremely active brain, and this brain can easily be diverted if such people are not able to enjoy the things that you and I enjoy in our way of life.
We are profiting by the conditions which are to some extent responsible for destitution. Hence we must look on the care of the incapacitated as a necessary expense which we are obliged to shoulder. We have almost no alternative in that case. We are obliged to shoulder that responsibility. Why? Because with the advent of urbanization, industrialization and such conditions, there are consequent changes in our economy and in many cases these are the causes.

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the discussion that has taken place is expected to be followed, as indeed several hon. members have suggested, by a statement from me as Minister of National Health and Welfare. In taking part in this debate, I propose first of all to indicate what is being done in the important field of rehabilitation, apart altogether from whatever cash benefits are received by various segments of the population of Canada.
It will be seen from this kind of review that a great deal is already being done by all levels of jurisdiction in this country regarding the important question raised in the resolution proposed by the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor). I think it would be advisable for us to recall the actual terms of the resolution, which reads:
That, In the opinion of this house, the government should consider the advisability of co-operating with the provincial governments for the purpose of providing pensions, equal to old age pensions, for all those who are incapacitated and unable to earn their living, regardless of age.
The house has already expressed its gratitude to the hon. member for Fort William for introducing this resolution at this time, and I am sure we all agree that much good can flow from a discussion, dispassionate and fair as this debate has been. It should not be forgotten that, in introducing family allowances, the veterans' charter, the national health program and in doing other things in these fields, this government has provided a background in health and welfare that should serve, and it must serve, as a proper basis for consideration of this particular problem.
All of the social services in Canada cannot and should not be designated for the sole competence of one governmental authority. . It would be wrong for the federal government
Pensions for Disabled Persons to assume full control and full interest in all phases of social welfare and of health activities. That is not only good government in a confederation such as ours, but it is also the view of the ten provincial governments of our country. As one who has to take part in conferences with the provinces from time to time, may I say that I have been reminded by those provincial authorities that there are fields of action which are peculiarly fitted for their interest; that there are fields in which there can be joint endeavour, but under no circumstances should we, in a country such as ours, seek to arrogate to Ottawa full authority and full and exclusive interest in all phases of welfare and health activity.
It must not be thought, however, that in saying that I am now preparing a complete defence against doing anything in the field of rehabilitation and providing cash benefits for our invalid population, or for those who are incapacitated and on that account unable to provide full maintenance for themselves and their families. For the fact is that while in Canada there is no single disability cash benefit scheme, there are nevertheless under various programs-mostly federal but also under provincial auspices-at the present time some 325,000 disabled Canadians who are receiving assistance at a cost of $110 million a year, almost 80 per cent of which is borne by the central authority. That is a considerable proportion of the population. It is a fact that has not been emphasized here today. Those who have argued for this proposition, and argued well, have failed, it seems to me, to emphasize the important contribution already being made not only by the provinces but by the federal government in this important matter.
It must not be forgotten that in 1952 there came into being in this country the most comprehensive old age security system of any country in the world, and that scheme has a very definite bearing on this matter. Likewise, in that same year, the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe), and I convoked a conference, which was held in the city of Toronto, on the question of rehabilitation, a very important prerequisite to a satisfactory system of disability pensions.
At that conference the ten provinces of Canada were represented, as well as the voluntary health and welfare agencies of the country, hospital, medical and allied professions, the three departments of the federal government, organized labour and management, universities, social welfare organizations and so on. The conclusion of that

Pensions for Disabled Persons conference was that in developing programs in this field careful consideration must be given to the place of disability allowances in the physical and vocational rehabilitation of the disabled. Consideration must likewise be given, of course, to the constitutional position, to administrative difficulties and to the relative priority of disability pensions in the over-all social security program.
I was interested in the observations of the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) who strongly supported this measure. I recalled at once the contributions which he made to the discussion, and they were valuable contributions, during the sittings of the committee on old age security in 1950. His observations will be found at pages 808 and 810-11 of the minutes of the committee. It will be found that throughout the deliberations of that committee the hon. gentleman emphasized the difficulty of using for the purpose of the receipt of cash benefits the yardstick of total disability. That merely emphasizes the point that was made at the conference in Toronto as to the administrative difficulties.
Now with regard to rehabilitation. As I said a moment ago, almost $11 million is made available to the provinces under crippled children, mental health and tuberculosis control grants. Very substantial proportions of this money are used for rehabilitation purposes. Then again, $100,000 a year is provided by the Department of National Health and Welfare to national voluntary agencies engaged in rehabilitation work. The department offers valuable consultative services to the provinces and to private agencies in such fields as blindness control and mental health. Federal-provincial aid is being given to special federal-provincial projects to provide surgical operations to restore the sight of selected blind pensioners.
Today I, along with many members of this house, received two delegations representing the various blind associations of our country.


They came to ask the government to give consideration to increasing the basic pension for the blind and to removing the means test. In dealing with this application I pointed out that these associations and the provincial and federal governments had been able to bring about a great improvement in social welfare measures in so far as they apply to the blind. When one is considering the particular question under discussion one would have to bear in mind our obligations to the blind as well as our obligations in other fields.
Likewise the federal government, through the Department of Veterans Affairs, provides welfare services and treatment for disabled veterans. That service includes rehabilitation activities as well as cash benefits for many thousands of veterans who come within the ambit of the resolution now under discussion.
Now with regard to the large segments of the population which are covered by provisions fully as generous as those envisaged in the resolution now before us, I would point out that all persons between the ages of 65 and 69 years with insufficient means to provide for their own needs are taken care of through federal-provincial old age assistance programs. Those 70 years of age and over are cared for under federal old age security legislation regardless of means. It is correct therefore to state that the objectives of this resolution are being already realized in so far as those of our population over 65 years of age are concerned.
Then with regard to blind persons, all adult blind persons regardless of age who are unable to earn their own living are taken care of under the new federal-provincial blind persons' allowance program. It is worth noting that the blind are the largest single group of civilian disabled, and represent perhaps one-third of the total number of those who are incapacitated.
With regard to our veterans, I think it is desirable to remember that all our veterans who served in both world wars are covered by provisions even more generous than those contemplated in the present resolution. Over 200,000 disabled veterans are now receiving assistance, either in the form of pensions or war veterans allowances.
At the provincial level there are a number of important provisions for the disabled. Everyone in this house knows that the provincial governments have developed comprehensive provisions for partial and total disability benefits under their workmen's compensation programs. In most provinces where a husband is prevented from working

by physical or mental disability aid is provided under a system of mothers' allowances. As an example of what is being done for tuberculosis victims, most provinces provide special allowances for persons incapacitated by that disease. At least one province, Alberta, has a provision for widows' pensions which covers a small segment of the disabled group below 65 years of age. Newfoundland has its dependents allowances act which takes care of the disabled, among others.
It is therefore clear that a large proportion of our disabled population, all those over 65 years of age, our war veterans, all our blind, those who have been injured by industrial accidents and other similar groups are covered already under one or other of the programs I have described.
Last year the province of Ontario went a step further in introducing a new plan for the disabled. The initiative which that province took seems to suggest that possibly disability pensions, like workmen's compensation and mothers' allowances, can best be taken care of by the provincial governments to the extent that they cannot be subject to insurance principles. I know that is the view of the government of Ontario from the discussions I have had with them.
It certainly is the view of at least three other governments that this is a field which they can best attend to, though they do not all agree that there should be no financial participation by the federal government. When we embarked upon the old age security program we had in mind the fact that we were assuming a greater responsibility, not only for those 70 years of age and over but for the group which would be covered under the new act, those between the ages of 65 and 70 years. We were relieving the provinces of a great financial responsibility. Their financial load has been very considerably reduced as a result of our old age security program.
To come back to the scheme in Ontario, I have not seen official figures as to the extent of that program. I understand that the number of recipients is not large and that consequently such a program is well within the capacity of the province. I hope to be able to announce the results of our health-sickness survey within a very few months, and that will reveal, I think, that this problem is not as great in the proportion of disabled people as might be thought, particularly when one takes into account the 350,000 individuals in the country who are now receiving cash benefits in one form or another through the federal government. It may be that the survey will reveal that, just as this group is within the capacity of the
Pensions for Disabled Persons province of Ontario financially, so too will it be well within the financial capacity of municipal and provincial governments throughout the country.
In any event it seems to me that these programs can best be handled provincially because there is a precedent already, and because of the heavy administrative problems involved, administrative difficulties which were ably pointed out in the old age security committee by the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Blair) a year ago. So with this in mind it might be well to note that the federal government's assumption of the total cost of old age security payments for those 70 and over has reduced provincial expenditures on old age pensions by more than $18 million a year, and our estimate would be that the kind of scheme envisaged by the proposition now before the house would certainly not cost the provinces anything like that in total. Because, it seems to me, we are now doing our share in respect of this problem and because we have other great obligations, I could not get up in the house at this time and accept this resolution without qualification, much as my own human instincts and sympathies, like those of every other hon. member, might lead me to do. I could not do that in the light of the situation which I am describing to the house, and also because of other things that the government yet hopes to be able to do in these wide humanitarian fields for the people of this country.
It is not that these things should not be done, and not that they will not be done. I firmly believe that the attitude taken by the province of Ontario will be emulated by other provinces in the period that lies ahead. Therefore it seems to me that we must look at the whole question in the light first of all of the kind of country in which we are living. There can be no argument about our unanimous wish to see that provision is made for the individual who is incapacitated to the point that he cannot provide for himself or his dependents. There is no doubt that he has a strong and justifiable demand for assistance at the hands of the community. Of that there can be no question. The question is what jurisdiction of government should bear the responsibility.
In answering, one will have to emphasize that the federal government has assumed the cost of family allowances, a burden of over $28 million a month, a social welfare measure bringing security to over four and a half million children in two million families every month, and has undertaken an old age security program that will cost well over $300 million this year, which cost will increase because of the increase in the ageing of our

Pensions for Disabled Persons population. It has assumed the cost of these two measures together with the national health program, the veterans charter and our contributions to the unemployment insurance scheme, as well as half the cost of old age assistance, and in addition there is the reserve of projects that the Canadian people will want to have in store for future action.
It seems to us that we can develop these schemes in partnership with the various provincial governments, and this is one phase of activity which I believe most of them are prepared to undertake and which I believe they can do better than we. The administrative difficulty is very great, as we have found in administering those problems of rehabilitation that come directly within our own sphere of activity.
I believe this discussion serves a useful purpose. Reference was made a few moments ago to the fact that I had been at the United Nations, and the hon. member who proposed the resolution was kind enough to speak of the work which I was able to do there. This is the first opportunity I have had to comment on that reference and I should like to make this observation, it being the first chance I have had in the house since my return from the seventh assembly.
Canada was honoured at that assembly in more ways than one, and perhaps in no more effective and impressive way than by the very able and constructive manner in which Canada's Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) carried out the assignment of president of the general assembly. One of the things that impresses the various delegations to the general assembly, as indeed it impresses anyone who attends the meetings of the various organs of the United Nations, is that there is a sound appreciation on the part of most countries of what Canada is doing in the field of health and welfare. That is particularly true, of course, at the economic and social council. It is true on the part of those who go to the world health organization, as the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. McCusker) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) have reminded the house.
When we come to consider suggestions such as are put forward today it is important for each of us to recognize what we have done in these fields and not to belittle the accomplishment. There has been no belittling of that accomplishment in any part of the house today. The debate has been on a high level and of high order. There has been a common recognition of the importance of the


problem, but perhaps not a sufficient appreciation of the extent of rehabilitation that is now going on in the country, and perhaps not a sufficient appreciation of the extent to which cash benefits are now being extended to so many people by one of the several government authorities in the country, the federal government.
Later in the session I hope to be able to announce a program in connection with a phase of activity in our department that will not be unrelated to this matter, although it will not be directly in answer to what is requested in the resolution. I must make it clear that it will not provide for disability pensions, but it will be a matter closely related to this problem and to many other phases of activity with which our department would normally be expected to be concerned.
I should like to take this opportunity to say to those who have made representations today and to the various organizations of the blind that the submissions they have made will receive the most careful consideration and attention at the hands of the government. The blind are one group of many in the category of disabled and incapacitated individuals in this country. It is the first group among the disabled to have received assistance at the hands of government in Canada on the federal level.
I think we can be proud of our achievements. I am not speaking only of the government, although I speak of it too because this government has great achievements to its credit over the course of the years in the field of health and welfare. I am speaking of the contribution that has been made in a co-operative way between those various groups and ourselves.
First of all, we have increased the basic pension three times. We have met almost 100 per cent the proposals put forward in the six-point program which the Canadian National Institute for the Blind offered to us three years ago. In every particular but one so far we have recognized their full demands.
On the other hand there is the work we have done in setting up, under the national health program, the glaucoma clinics, the remedial surgery program that is going on in this country to improve the sight of the blind. These are programs of the first order, about which perhaps not sufficient has been said.
I might take this opportunity of urging those provinces in the country that have not agreed with us on this remedial surgery program not to delay but to come in so that we can provide relief for many blind

pensioners who can yet have their sight restored by capable and effective surgical operation. Under that scheme the federal government pays 75 per cent of the total cost involved, and I am happy to say that in 70 individual surgical operations on people who were receiving blind pensions, and whose hope for the restoration of their eyesight had long been given up, we were able to effect under this program significant restoration of sight in over 40 cases. That kind of program is one we want to see continued, and it is one that is closely related to this whole question of rehabilitation.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we set up under the program conceived by the former minister of labour and now ably carried on by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), in conjunction with the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe) and myself as Minister of National Health and Welfare, a scheme by which we sought to provide for co-ordination in the field of rehabilitation of the handicapped and incapacitated of our country. We have set up a national advisory committee composed of the representatives of organizations in the country best suited by tradition and knowledge to deal with this problem. In addition to that we have appointed as coordinating officer with residence here in Ottawa, serving in the Department of Labour, the former head of the workmen's compensation board rehabilitation service in the province of Ontario. It is his job to try to develop a program in conjunction with the provinces both for the rehabilitation and for the financial assistance, in time, of those who through no fault of their own find themselves incapacitated. That is a scheme which is based on the kind of programs other countries have followed. I believe it marks a very definite step in what we are doing both in terms of meeting the proposal that is before us today and also in effecting and completing what we are doing for the rehabilitation of the incapacitated and for others in the country.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Question.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: My hon. friend says "question" and I want to say to him that the big question that is before us today-

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us have the vote.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: -is whether or not we have gone too far in this country.
Let us have a vote.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Speaking for the government I want to say this. The government of this country is firmly of the view that there cannot be too much interest in humanitarian questions.
Pensions for Disabled Persons
As long as it does not come to a vote.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: This government and this party will always support the interests of suffering humanity.
The vote?

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) obviously is not interested in these problems that have to do with human welfare, otherwise he would let me point this out. While I believe the kind of society that he advocates is one that possesses within itself the seed of its own destruction, I do say that those who argue against the welfare state make a tremendous mistake. If by "welfare state" they wish to put the emphasis on "state", then, of course, I agree with the suggestion and deplore the sinister implications involved in the phrase. But, if by "welfare state" we mean that the government of the country should be concerned with the welfare of its people, then I am unashamedly a strong protagonist of the welfare state.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Let us have a vote then.
So is the government of which I am a member and it is because of that conviction-
That you are talking it out.

-that this government has brought in family allowances, the veterans' charter, old age security and the national health program. It is because of that it has been able to effect a measure of co-operation with the provincial governments that as Minister of National Health and Welfare I am justified-
In talking this out.

-in saying to the hon. gentleman who proposed this resolution that it has at least served the purpose of giving all of us an opportunity to appreciate the great progress that has been made in the field of health and welfare in this most favoured among the nations of the world.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You have talked it out again.
